title: Happiness Revisited
coreMove: Stop treating improved circumstances as the route to happiness and identify where inner order must be built directly.
sourcePressure: The opening reset: material progress, comfort, and rising expectations have not secured happiness, so the problem becomes control over experience rather than better circumstances alone.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Turn the opening into generic anti-materialism or gratitude advice.

sourceAnchors.name: Aristotle
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen source notes that the book opens with Aristotle and the human question of happiness
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Aristotle belongs at the doorway because the question is old: people have always wanted happiness, and still keep mistaking its address.

hook: open with a named person staring at a phone and realizing the abstract lesson
start with comfort versus challenge in slogan form
counterintuition: Most people assume X, but actually Y
The real problem is not X, it is Y
You do not need more discipline, you need better systems
tryThisNow: Set a timer and reflect on your life
Write down three things you learned
Notice your attention without changing the situation
examples: timestamp plus protagonist plus laptop plus decision in every case
generic office, classroom, kitchen, commute rotation
same visible beat with different props

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a product manager after a promotion announcement
exampleSpecs.audience: newly promoted knowledge workers who expected relief
exampleSpecs.stakes: she has the title and the raise but the train ride home feels flatter than before
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she closes the congratulatory email, leaves the salary tab open, and chooses whether to add another purchase to the wishlist or block a demanding design problem for the morning
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The commuter train window throws office lights back at her face

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital scheduler redesigning his evenings after overtime
exampleSpecs.audience: workers who confuse exhaustion relief with a good life
exampleSpecs.stakes: his free night is rare and can become either passive collapse or a chosen absorbing activity
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: contrast the old evening of scrolling in scrubs with the night he sets up a difficult model kit and notices the hour disappear
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Daniel four Thursdays to admit the couch was not restoring him

exampleSpecs.domain: a first-year student staring at perfect grades and no satisfaction
exampleSpecs.audience: high achievers who mistake outcomes for experience quality
exampleSpecs.stakes: she risks losing the point of study to grade-chasing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: her tutor asks which assignment she would keep doing if nobody posted marks, and Camille has to choose a real project instead of another grade tactic
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Which one would you still do without the grade?"

exampleSpecs.domain: a retired engineer with a paid-off house and empty mornings
exampleSpecs.audience: people who reached a promised milestone and still feel restless
exampleSpecs.stakes: his planned comfort is turning into aimless time
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: ask whether the quiet calendar will feel like freedom or drift, then show him testing one structured woodworking challenge against a blank morning
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What happens when the calendar finally stops demanding anything?

exampleSpecs.domain: a new parent trying to buy her way out of anxiety
exampleSpecs.audience: parents pressured by gear and comparison
exampleSpecs.stakes: another purchase may deepen the same restless loop
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you stand in a baby store aisle and notice the promised calm moving one shelf farther away, then choose a tiny shared ritual over another item
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You are holding the third sleep gadget and still checking reviews

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum volunteer replacing passive Sundays with sketching duty
exampleSpecs.audience: older adults and weekend drifters who need structured engagement
exampleSpecs.stakes: his free time is abundant but thin unless attention has a task
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he sharpens one pencil, chooses a single sculpture, and measures its shadow line for forty minutes instead of wandering the galleries
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Graphite dust marks the side of his thumb

skillTargets: separating external improvement from inner order
spotting when comfort is being asked to do the work of engagement
keeping structural hardship distinct from the narrower flow claim

tryThisNowSpec: Name one upgrade you keep expecting to make life feel settled, then write the experience it is supposed to create and one way to practice that experience today.
